items.hint: the everyday verb — the physical action
items.note: The default word for swimming anywhere: a pool, the sea, a dog swimming. Compare すいえいをします (suiei o shimasu), which frames it as a sport.
すいえい (suiei) is swimming as a discipline — lessons, clubs, competitions. しゅみは すいえい です (shumi wa suiei desu) = 'my hobby is swimming'.

items.target: もういちどおねがいします
items.note: Built from おねがいします (onegaishimasu), already used for よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu). もう いちど (mō ichido) = 'one more time'.
Stands alone as a pronoun. When a noun follows, switch to この (kono): この ほん (kono hon).
Near the listener, not near you: これ (kore) is by you, あれ (are) is far from both.
Away from both of you. これ (kore) is by me, それ (sore) is by you, あれ (are) is over there.
Also means 'this way / this direction'. Already met in こちらは イギリスの ライアンです (kochira wa Igirisu no Ryan desu), where it introduces a person politely.
Polite counterpart of それ (sore); also 'that way'.
Polite counterpart of あれ (are); also 'over that way'.
Never stands alone — これ (kore) is the one that does. この かばん (kono kaban) = 'this bag'.
Pairs with それ (sore) the way この (kono) pairs with これ (kore).
Pairs with あれ (are). あの ひと (ano hito) = 'that person over there'.
Written は but pronounced わ (wa) when it marks the topic — the single most common reading trap in kana.

items.target: わたしはがくせいです
items.note: The は here is read わ (wa). がくせい (gakusei) was introduced with the other occupations.
Pronounced お (o). It only ever appears as a particle — never inside a word.
を (o) marks what the verb acts on: すし (sushi) is the thing being eaten.
Covers sweets, snacks and confectionery generally.
The animal and the food alike.
ぎゅう (gyū) 'cow' + にく (niku) 'meat'. Same pattern builds とりにく (toriniku) 'chicken'.
Contrast ビル (biru), an office building — the long-vowel ー is the only thing telling them apart.
Wasei-eigo from 'PET bottle' — a disposable plastic drinks bottle, not a pet's bottle.
A な-adjective despite ending in い: きれいな へや (kirei na heya). Means both 'pretty' and 'clean'.
Irregular: negative かっこよくない (kakko yokunai), past かっこよかった (kakko yokatta).
Spelled おお (ō), not おう — one of the few words that keeps おお.
A な-adjective: とうめいな コップ (tōmei na koppu) = 'a clear glass'. The final い belongs to めい, it isn't an い-adjective ending.
One of only two colours that work both ways: きいろい シャツ (kiiroi shatsu) and きいろの シャツ (kiiro no shatsu) are both correct.
Literally 'tea-colour'. Like きいろ (kiiro), it takes either form: ちゃいろい くつ (chairoi kutsu) or ちゃいろの くつ (chairo no kutsu).
みどり (midori) is a noun, so it needs の to describe something: みどりの くるま (midori no kuruma). There is no みどりい.

items.reviewNote: Added to answer your question about which colours need の. しろ is NOT の-only — しろい is a normal い-adjective.
items.note: Only four colours have a native い-form: あかい (akai), あおい (aoi), しろい (shiroi), くろい (kuroi). Everything else needs の.

items.reviewNote: Added to answer your question about which colours need の. くろ is NOT の-only — くろい is a normal い-adjective.
items.note: くろい くつ (kuroi kutsu) = 'black shoes'. Directly modifies the noun, unlike みどりの (midori no).

items.reviewNote: Added as a second example of a colour that only works with の, per your question.
items.note: A noun like みどり (midori), so it needs の: むらさきの はな (murasaki no hana). There is no むらさきい.

items.reviewNote: Added as an example of a loanword colour, which is always の-only.
items.note: Loanword colours are always nouns: ピンクの かばん (pinku no kaban).

items.reviewNote: Added as an example of a loanword colour, which is always の-only.
items.note: The colour and the fruit share the word. オレンジの ぼうし (orenji no bōshi).

items.reviewNote: Added as a further の-only colour; グレー (gurē) is the equally common loanword form.
items.note: Literally 'ash colour'. グレー (gurē) is the loanword alternative and is just as common.
Wasei-eigo. Not a 'trainer' (a person) and not British 'trainers' (shoes) — it's a crewneck sweatshirt.
Not an English 'parka' (a heavy winter coat) — パーカー (pākā) is a hooded sweatshirt.
Not the English 'muffler' (a car part) — in clothing it's a winter neck scarf.
Covers hats and caps alike. Note the long vowel: ぼう (bō), not ぼ.
くつ (kutsu) 'shoe' + した (shita) 'under'.
No sound change — it stays さ (sa), unlike the floor counter where さんがい (sangai) does shift.
さつ (satsu) counts bound things — books, magazines, notebooks. いち (ichi) shortens to いっ (i-) here.
Textbooks teach なんがい (nangai). なんかい (nankai) is also heard, but it collides with 'how many times'.
よん (yon), never し (shi), for this counter.
きゅう (kyū), not く (ku), for this counter.
じゅう (jū) shortens to じゅっ (ju-).
Japanese counts from street level, so いっかい (ikkai) is the British ground floor. The British 'first floor' is にかい (nikai).
ろく (roku) shortens to ろっ (ro-).
The one that changes sound: か becomes が. さんかい (sankai) would mean 'three times', not 'third floor'.
はち (hachi) shortens to はっ (ha-).
じょう (jō) marks a place or ground — the same ending turns up in other venue words.
Shares the じょう (jō) 'place' ending with ちゅうしゃじょう (chūshajō).
Literally 'hand-washing place' (お + てあらい, o + tearai) — the polite word for a toilet.
Turns up inside てんとうむし (tentōmushi), 'ladybird'.
A position word: ~の よこ (no yoko) = 'beside ~'. いすの よこ (isu no yoko) = 'next to the chair'.
Japanese doesn't split crocodile from alligator — わに (wani) covers both.
